title: Introduction
text: Hello. This is my Digital Banking Core Platform, the engine of a bank.
It has accounts, money transfers, a ledger that always balances, and identity checks.
It is built with Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, Flyway, Kafka and Keycloak.
In the next ten minutes I will cover the problem, the design, three hard challenges, the results, and what I would do next.

title: The problem
text: A bank core has to get four things right.
First, it must never lose or invent money. Every transfer is a debit and a credit that cancel out.
Second, it must never charge twice. If a network failure makes the app retry, the money must not move again.
Third, it must stay correct under load, even when many requests hit one account at the same moment.
And fourth, it must know who is who: login, roles, and identity checks before anyone can move money.

title: Double-entry bookkeeping
text: The foundation is double-entry bookkeeping. Money is never just added or subtracted.
Every movement is two entries that cancel out. A debit is stored as a negative number and a credit as a positive number.
Here Alice sends two thousand five hundred to Bob. Minus 2,500 for Alice, plus 2,500 for Bob, and the sum is zero.

This is enforced three ways. One service is the only code that writes entries. A database trigger rejects any unbalanced transaction at commit. And the ledger is append-only, so history can never be edited.
So the sum of every entry in the whole bank is always exactly zero.

title: Architecture
text: Here is the architecture. Clients log in at Keycloak and receive a signed token.
They call the Spring Boot application with that token. A security filter verifies it and the controllers check the role.
The services hold the business rules, and the repositories run explicit SQL against PostgreSQL, which is the source of truth.
Kafka is reached only through an outbox, which I will explain later, so Kafka being down never blocks a transfer.

title: Data model
text: The data model is managed by Flyway migrations, applied in order, exactly once each.
Customers own accounts. A transaction produces ledger entries, one per side. The idempotency keys table points back to the transaction it produced.
Money is stored as NUMERIC with two decimals, never floating point.
The account balance is a cached total. The ledger is the truth. And a database check stops an ordinary account from ever going below zero.

title: Life of one transfer
text: This is the life of one transfer, and all of it is one database transaction.
I reserve the idempotency key. I check the caller owns the source account and that their KYC is approved.
I lock both accounts in a fixed order, run the fraud rules, check funds, and write the transaction with its debit and credit.
I update both balances, write the event to the outbox table, store the result on the key, and commit.
If anything fails, everything rolls back, so there is never a half-finished transfer.

title: Challenge 1: concurrency
text: The first challenge is many requests at once.
A lost update happens when two transfers both read a balance of 1,000 and each spend 600. Without a lock both succeed. I lock both account rows before reading.
A deadlock happens when a transfer from A to B and one from B to A each hold one lock and wait for the other. I always lock in ascending account id, so one simply waits.
In my database-level check, 30 parallel transfers of 100 from a balance of 1,000 gave exactly 10 successes and 20 insufficient funds. And 40 simultaneous opposite transfers produced zero deadlocks.

title: Challenge 2: idempotency
text: The second challenge is that retries must never double-charge.
The client sends the same Idempotency-Key on every retry. I insert that key in the same transaction as the money movement, so the key exists if and only if the transfer committed.
A retry finds the key and returns the original result. The same key with a different amount is refused. A failed request leaves no key, so it can be retried.
In my check, 20 simultaneous identical requests produced one transfer and 19 replays, and the account was debited once.

title: Challenge 3: events
text: The third challenge is telling Kafka without losing events.
A database and Kafka cannot share one transaction. So I write the event to an outbox table inside the money transaction.
A background publisher sends the rows to Kafka and waits for the acknowledgement. A consumer turns them into notifications and ignores duplicates by event id.
So there is never an event for a rolled-back transfer, never a lost event for a committed one, and transfers keep working even if Kafka is down.

title: Identity and safety
text: Now identity and safety.
Keycloak handles login. My application never sees a password. It verifies the signed token on every call, and customers can only see their own accounts.
The KYC workflow goes from submit to review to approve or reject. Nobody can open an account or transfer money until approved, and nobody can review their own KYC.
Fraud rules block a very large single transfer, a daily total over the limit, and too many transfers in a minute. Every block is logged for compliance.

title: Results
text: Now the results, and I want to be precise about what they show.
My database-level concurrency script passed all nine checks on PostgreSQL 16, ending with a reconciliation where the ledger sums to zero, with no unbalanced transaction and no balance mismatch.
I also wrote 32 Java integration tests that run against a real PostgreSQL in Docker.
The throughput of 228 transfers per second came from a replay of the transfer SQL on a small sandbox. It shows the database design behaves. It is not a benchmark of the Spring application.

title: Next steps
text: Finally, the limits and next steps.

All cash operations lock one cash account, so I would shard it per branch. It supports one currency, so foreign exchange needs a conversion account. There are no reversals yet, only the schema support.
Fraud rules are static thresholds, so I would train a scoring model. The Keycloak setup is demo-grade, so production needs authorization code with PKCE and TLS. And I would upgrade to Spring Boot 4.
Thank you. I am happy to take questions.
